# TITLE
LINUX SECURITY HANDBOOK

# SUBTITLE
6. SUDO AND PRIVILEGE ESCALATION SECURITY

PAGE 6 OF 20

# BODY_PARAGRAPHS

**ROOT ACCESS RISKS**
Root has unlimited power on the system.
A single mistake or compromise can lead to full system takeover.
Limit and monitor root access carefully.

**/ETC/SUDOERS**
Main sudo configuration file.
Controls which users or groups can run which commands as root or another user.
Always edit with visudo, never a text editor.

**/ETC/SUDOERS.D/**
Directory for additional sudo configuration files.
Used to add custom rules without modifying the main sudoers file.
Each file in this directory is included automatically.

**VISUDO**
Safe way to edit sudoers files.
Syntax is checked before saving.
Prevents locking yourself out of sudo access.
Always use: visudo or visudo -f <file>

**COMMAND-SPECIFIC SUDO ACCESS**
Grant users access to only the commands they need.
Example: Allow restart of specific services without full root access.
Reduces the attack surface.

**DANGEROUS SUDO CONFIGURATIONS**
Avoid broad permissions and wildcard commands.
Dangerous examples:
• ALL=(ALL) ALL
• ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
• Command wildcards like /bin/*
These can lead to full privilege escalation.

**NOPASSWD RISKS**
NOPASSWD allows running commands without entering a password.
If misconfigured, attackers can escalate privileges without any authentication.
Use only when absolutely necessary.

**REVIEWING SUDO PRIVILEGES**
Regularly review who has sudo access and what they can run.
Remove unused or excessive privileges.
Use audit logs to monitor sudo activity.

**LEAST-PRIVILEGE ADMINISTRATION**
Grant only the minimum access required.
Remove elevated access when not needed.
Use groups, command restrictions, and logging to enforce least-privilege principles.

# IMPORTANT_FILES
| File Path | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| /etc/sudoers | Main sudo configuration file. Controls which users or groups can run which commands as root or another user. |
| /etc/sudoers.d/ | Directory for additional sudo configuration files. Used to add custom rules without modifying the main sudoers file. |

# TABLES
## Sudo Command Examples Table
| Command | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| sudo -l | List allowed sudo commands for current user |
| sudo -ll | List all privileges in detail |
| sudo -u \<user\> \<command\> | Run command as another user |
| visudo | Edit /etc/sudoers safely |
| visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/\<file\> | Edit a file in sudoers.d directory |
| sudo -k | Invalidate password timestamp (next sudo will ask password) |
| sudo -v | Refresh the sudo timestamp (extend login session) |

## Sudo Security Checklist Table
| Checklist Item |
| :--- |
| Limit users with sudo access |
| Use command-specific permissions |
| Avoid NOPASSWD unless required |
| Do not use wildcards carelessly |
| Review /etc/sudoers regularly |
| Audit sudo usage in logs |
| Remove unnecessary privileges |
| Use least-privilege principles |
| Test configurations before deployment |

# COMMANDS
1. **Command:** `sudo -l`
   **Description:** List allowed sudo commands for current user
   
2. **Command:** `sudo -ll`
   **Description:** List all privileges in detail
   
3. **Command:** `sudo -u <user> <command>`
   **Description:** Run command as another user
   
4. **Command:** `visudo`
   **Description:** Edit /etc/sudoers safely
   
5. **Command:** `visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/<file>`
   **Description:** Edit a file in sudoers.d directory
   
6. **Command:** `sudo -k`
   **Description:** Invalidate password timestamp (next sudo will ask password)
   
7. **Command:** `sudo -v`
   **Description:** Refresh the sudo timestamp (extend login session)

# TIPS_NOTES_WARNINGS
- Always edit with visudo, never a text editor.
- Always use: visudo or visudo -f <file>
- Avoid broad permissions and wildcard commands.
- Use only when absolutely necessary [referring to NOPASSWD].
